512.t: Morgan State and the Baltimore scene with Gary Bartz
512.s: Only classical theory at college, but Baltimore's Royal Theater and Pennsylvania Avenue were alive with jazz; he played standards with Gary Bartz at the North End Lounge.
512.q: Just basic classical theory. Because back then, when I was back there they hadn’t even started these jazz colleges and universities yet. But at that time in Baltimore, Maryland it was very, very musical. And all the jazz groups used to come down and play on Pennsylvania Avenue and so Baltimore was…

512.t: Learning tunes on the bandstand in Baltimore jam sessions
512.s: Jam sessions at the North End Lounge were a second school; older players and bass players called out changes.
512.q: So it’s just basic standards. I wasn’t writing back then. So but the North End Lounge, all the jazz groups when they came in town they would come by and do jam sessions. So like you know, so I was really in school in another way, both schools at the same time.

786.t: Learning the blues in the Raven Avenue red-light district
786.s: Shade grew up in a red-light district on Raven Avenue where pianos played blues day and night, including Handy's tunes.
786.ch: Beale Street and the early Memphis scene
786.q: What neighborhood was this? That was on Raven Avenue, just between Beale and Lennon on Raven. Used to call it Haddon's Avenue long years back. Used to be a gang of sporting people hanging around there and piano would be running night and day playing all kind of blues, Handys blues, St. Louis blues,…

850.t: Playing every night at the Car 54 club in Heidelberg
850.s: Berger was house pianist at a Heidelberg club where Army and Air Force jazzmen like Cedar Walton, Lex Humphries and Don Ellis sat in; learning tunes by ear and the value of playing nightly versus classroom study.
850.q: Yeah I would say so. And also one lucky streak that I had was that Heidelberg had a little club called the Car 54, and the surrounding Army and Air Force stations had all bands. And in those bands played a few jazz musicians who later became pretty well known, such as Cedar Walton or Lex Humphries…

559.t: Playboy Club trio with Monty Alexander and Bob Cranshaw
559.s: At the Playboy Club he was musically beaten up nightly by Alexander and Cranshaw, learning harmony and tunes on the job.
559.ch: Playboy Club and the working life
559.q: on songs, no. I didn’t work on songs. But when I first started playing I worked at — I got a job at the Playboy Club. It came through another guitar player who was leaving and it was a trio job, it was guitar, bass, and piano. The piano player was Monty Alexander and the bass player was Bob…

616.t: Gigging by ear at fourteen in the late 1950s
616.s: He played weddings and club dates by ear at 14, learning standards and song form.
616.q: Yeah. Well it just kind of worked out that way — whether it was providence made me do that, but all I remember is we had an exceptional high school music program and the local band director actually was a local musician and when I was 14 years old I was out playing gigs with the older guys. So I…

670.t: First tour, the Onyx Club, and learning from musicians
670.s: She played small clubs and theaters, then went to the Onyx Club on 52nd Street; musicians helped her though she does not read music.
670.q: Small clubs and the theaters. We did the theater in Chicago and the Apollo of course when we came back to New York. And then Ella Johnson went back with the band. And then I went to 52nd Street to the Onyx Club. Hot Lips Page took me down there and the musicians have helped me all through my…

657.t: Wally's Cafe in Boston and learning the form
657.s: Weekly gig at Wally's where older rhythm sections tested him; advice to know the form of a tune.
657.ch: Boston, Berklee and the band family
657.q: Definitely. Also to find people to come to play with. Also all throughout that I was playing several other types of gigs like wedding gigs and, you know, working at this place called Wally’s in Boston, it was like a weekly gig for me, Wally’s Café. And that was sort of a school outside of the…

343.t: Clarence Love's Lounge and learning tunes by ear
343.s: Playing blues in B flat, then Clarence Love's Lounge, with Tulsa's big band scene; he learned standards in a year.
343.q: No. You just started playing and you heard it. And usually the blues were in B flat. B flat 7. Like a boogie woogie kind of sound.

660.t: Learning tunes to sit in: Rusty's in Toledo and Eddie Abrams
660.s: Ries explains how he learned tunes sitting in at Rusty's club in Toledo with Eddie Abrams, Claude Black and other Detroit musicians.
660.q: Well luckily there was a really cool jazz club in Toledo, Ohio called Rusty’s. Her name was Rusty Monroe, and she had this club for many, many, many years. And she cooked the food. And I think I remember once like as she got older and she was telling me about how long it took for her to actually…

557.t: The jam session where a waltz exposed him: lesson from Donald Bailey
557.s: At an early jam session he played four-four against a three-four tune, and Donald Bailey explained odd measures to him.
557.q: Well when I first started to play man, before I played my first gig I would practice and practice because I didn’t go to, I couldn’t afford to go to school, so I learned from friends you know, and we’d play. And I went to this jam session one time, and I mean you’re talking about embarrassing, man,…

851.t: Erroll Garner's quartet at the Stage Door Canteen
851.s: As a high school senior he led the house trio with Walter Lastie and received piano lessons from Garner during a two-week booking.
851.ch: Early New Orleans experiences and sideman roles
851.q: Well in my senior year of high school I had a gig with Walter Lastie, it was my gig but Walter Lastie was the drummer. He was one of Herlin Riley’s uncles, and we had a band when Herlin Riley played trumpet. He played trumpet before he played drums. And a bass player, and Sam Alcorn, a great…

852.t: Learning standards on cruise ships and settling in Pittsburgh
852.s: Older ship musicians taught him tunes before the internet; he later moved to Pittsburgh with a cover band and met Roger Humphries.
852.q: Learned how to be punctual. Learned how to front a band. Learned a bunch of standards without the internet and real books or anything. Nineties.

61.t: Inheriting Collector's Corner from Stearns; collector Hoyt Kline
61.s: Stearns handed over the New York news and Collector's Corner column; Avakian gained encyclopedic knowledge of records.
61.ch: Yale, Stearns and the big bands
61.q: He sure did. Not long after he said, “I think I’ll just keep reviewing records,” which I was sorry to hear him say, because I wanted to get free records. But he said, “Why don’t you do all the other stuff?” Get the New York news to him once a month and write the “Collector’s Corner” column. He…

503.t: Elvin's guitar and Downstairs; Detroit as a university without walls
503.s: Elvin taught him the folk-blues tune that became Downstairs; Burrell calls the Detroit scene a university.
503.q: “Downstairs.” But the original title was “Foxes and the Hounds.” That was like his thing, you know, the hounds chasing the foxes, you know. And, you know, that’s old country stuff there and that’s what it sounds like. So we had a discussion about it when I was making the record, I said, “I know,…

515.t: Transcribing Horace Silver and the high school trio
515.s: He learns by transcribing Horace Silver records and Blue Mitchell solos, forms a trio, and opens for Herb Pomeroy at the Stables.
515.q: Absolutely. I wanted to play like Bud right away, but it was too fast and too beyond me at first. So when... I loved everything that Miles and Bird did, but I couldn’t quite grasp it. The first grasp I had in really learning and duplicating one of my heroes’ music was Horace—and Horace’s quintet…

589.t: First gig with Burton's band, and learning blues and rhythm changes
589.s: At his first dance he cannot play the Parker blues or standards, is sent to sit out, and Burton then teaches him changes and sends him to Lyon and Healy to hear Shearing, Peterson and Powell.
589.q: remember all the names. Francisco played guitar. Redd Holt played drums. Eldee Young played bass. And here I am on piano, seven pieces. Booker Porter played the other tenor saxophone. “Okay, let’s take – let’s open some – about here. Let’s play a Charlie Parker piece. Ramsey, it’s just based on…

492.t: Before leaving Memphis: playing every night
492.s: Newton asks about Booker Little; Lloyd says he played every night from age ten or twelve, a difference from young musicians today.
492.ch: Booker Little and the Manassas circle
492.q: No, well the thing about - see here’s the thing: I went to Melrose at eighth grade, and I was playing with these blues bands and stuff. Then Phineas put me in his father’s band, then Willy Mitchell put me in his band after Phineas had left town, and I played all over with him. But I played every…

90.t: Paradise Alley and meeting Yusef Lateef
90.s: The St. Antoine and Adams clubs where saxophonists jammed, and where he taught Yusef Lateef (then Bill Evans) his first chord changes.
90.q: But anyway, getting back to the music. Down in Paradise Alley, that's where the action was. The Turf Club was there on St. Antoine. They had the D&C across the street, where we used to go over there and jam. And they had some very well-known saxophone players who used to play around there. A guy…
